title: Roman Numeral Workshop
context: Grade 4, the closing topic. An adult sees a conversion table. What the page is actually doing is teaching a system whose rules exclude far more than they allow, so the useful knowledge is which combinations are not numerals at all.

writeup.why: Write numbers the way a clock face does, using seven letters and three rules.
writeup.look: A tray of lettered tiles with their values underneath, and a rail above where the numeral is built.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Roman Numeral Workshop' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: what the rail is worth so far, in ink, rewritten every time a tile lands or leaves, with the number of tiles on the rail counted beside it; it is the one place the total is written, and it never reads as a score. On the third and fourth phases a second line under it counts the refusals and names the rule of the last one. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The build rail is 860 by 150 at 64,232, a ruled rail on the paper colour with a stop drawn at its left hand end; a tile that lands takes its place on the rail at 84 by 108 at a pitch of 92, so nine tiles fit along it and the longest numeral this chapter asks for fits exactly. The ledger is 226 by 150 at 924,232: one line per tile in the order they landed, the letter and the amount it brings, with a bar drawn at the left of each line, and a line that takes away carries its bar drawn back to front, so adding and subtracting are told apart by shape before any colour; a subtractive pair on the rail is ringed amber, because that pair is what settles the reading. The refusal strip is 860 by 64 at 64,398 and stands empty until a tile is refused, when it prints the rule that refused it in words with the refused tile drawn hollow at its left edge; the place on the rail that tile wanted is left as a hollow outline, so what was refused and where it wanted to go are both still on the stage. The reference card is 226 by 330 at 924,398, seven ruled rows, letter at the left and value at the right, in order of value, and it never closes; its back carries the six subtractive pairs and turns over on the fourth phase. The direction switch is 220 by 64 at 64,488, number into numeral at one end and numeral into number at the other, and the target card is 620 by 64 at 304,488, holding whichever of the two the phase has asked for. The tray is 860 by 150 at 64,580 with seven tiles 108 by 108 at a pitch of 120 from x 74, each letter in ink at 72 tall with its value under it; a tile drawn out of the tray leaves its outline behind and the outline refills at once, because the tray never runs out and no letter is ever used up. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across where a numeral has to be read back as a number, on the first, second and third phases; where a number has to be built the numeral is built on the rail itself and the pad carries the seven letter keys instead, in order of value, which drop that tile onto the right hand end of the rail. On the fourth phase the letter keys stay and a strip of the six allowed pairs sits under them, so a pair can be dropped as one press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the ones period is deep blue, the thousands period green, the lakhs period vermilion and the millions period rose; whatever settles the answer on this stage is amber; a zero that is only holding a place open is grey; and chrome never borrows one of them, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
writeup.finish: The card shows the numerals the child built, and the combinations the rules refused with the reason beside each one.

phases.win: every tile has been matched to its value at least once
phases.does: matches each letter to its value and drops single tiles into the rail
phases.goal: every Roman numeral is built from seven letters and no others
phases.says: Seven letters, and no more. Find the one worth fifty.
phases.check: Without looking at the card, which letter is worth fifty, and which one is worth five hundred?
phases.feels: there is nothing here to work out, only something to know
phases.hands: Copy the seven letters and their values onto a card by hand, in order of value, and leave the card on the table for the rest of the topic; then cover the values with a finger and read the letters off it.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many letters are there altogether? Second rung, the phase's: which of them is nearest in value to the one you want? Third rung: the tray is cut to three tiles with their values showing and the child picks from those. The reference card stays open behind all three, because this is a lookup and not a puzzle.

wrong.why: every other number in the chapter has had a way of being written, so a value as ordinary as this looks as though it must have a letter of its own.
wrong.move: hunts the tray for a letter worth twenty and finds nothing to pick up.
wrong.screen: the seven tiles lift a little together and set themselves down in order of value, and the steps between the values light one after another, one, then five, then ten, then fifty, so the gaps are shown to be part of the system. The rail keeps whatever is already on it.

wrong.why: everything else in this chapter has been worked out from something else, so guessing feels like the right kind of effort to be making.
wrong.move: works out what a letter is worth from the letter before it rather than reading it off the card.
wrong.screen: the reference card draws itself open row by row down the right of the working area, letter and value, and the row for the letter in hand lights and stays lit while the tile is held. Nothing on the rail is touched and nothing is marked.

phases.screen: the tray of seven tiles with the reference card open beside it
phases.soWhat: Seven letters carry fixed values, and every numeral is built from those seven and no others.
phases.concept: Seven letters do all the work

phases.win: the numeral reads correctly and the running total matches
phases.does: drops smaller tiles to the right and watches the total climb
phases.goal: a smaller letter to the right of a bigger one is added
phases.says: Put the smaller one on the right. Watch the total go up.
phases.check: Read this numeral to me, and for each letter say whether you added it or took it away, and why.
phases.feels: the order the tiles sit in turns out to be the whole of the reading
phases.hands: Lay two coins of different value on the table with the bigger one at the left, then add a third coin to the right of them, and say the running total out loud as each one goes down.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which side of the bigger letter is the smaller one standing on? Second rung, the phase's: does that side add or take away? Third rung: the rail is cut to two tiles and the child gives the total for that pair alone. The reference card and the pad stay open.

wrong.why: taking away is the rule that gets the most attention, and smallness looks like the thing it depends on.
wrong.move: takes the smaller letter away wherever it is standing, because it is the smaller one.
wrong.screen: the pair on the rail is ringed amber and the ring is drawn round the smaller tile's place rather than round the tile itself, so it is the side it stands on that lights; the ledger line for that tile is rewritten with its bar the right way round and the total climbs to what it should be. The child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the total comes to the same whichever order the letters are added in, and so it does.
wrong.move: builds the numeral with the small letters first, writing it up from its smallest part.
wrong.screen: the tiles slide along the rail into order of value, the biggest at the left, without one of them leaving the rail; the ledger rewrites itself in the new order with the same total standing at its foot, and the rule prints under the rail that a numeral is written from the biggest letter down.

phases.screen: the rail holding a bigger tile with space to its right
phases.soWhat: A smaller letter to the right of a bigger one is added, and a numeral is written from the biggest letter down.
phases.concept: A smaller letter on the right is added

phases.win: the fourth tile is refused and the rule is named on screen
phases.does: tries to add a fourth of the same letter and reads the refusal
phases.goal: repetition means addition, and three is the limit
phases.says: Try one more of the same. What does the rule card say?
phases.check: Why is forty not written as four of the ten letter, and what is it written as instead?
phases.feels: the arithmetic works perfectly and the numeral is still not allowed
phases.hands: Write four of the same letter in a row on paper and say its value out loud four times over, then look along the rule card together and cross the row out.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many of that letter are already on the rail? Second rung, the phase's: what does the rule card give as the limit? Third rung: the rail is left holding three of the letter and the tray offers only the tiles that could lawfully come next. The rule card stays open and nothing on the rail is taken away.

wrong.why: three of them added up perfectly well, so a fourth ought to add up too, and the arithmetic of it is not wrong.
wrong.move: drops a fourth tile of the same letter onto the rail.
wrong.screen: the tile stops a tile's height above the place it wanted and hangs there while the refusal strip prints the rule, that a letter may be repeated three times at most; the three tiles already down are left exactly as they are, and the fourth lifts back to the tray leaving its outline hollow in the gap.

wrong.why: the rule just met allowed three of a letter, so two of anything looks safely inside it.
wrong.move: drops a second of one of the three letters that are never repeated.
wrong.screen: the refusal strip prints the second rule, that this letter is never repeated at all, and the reference card draws a small bar under each of the three letters it covers; the rail keeps the first tile and the pair the child wanted is drawn hollow beside it.

phases.screen: the rail holding three of one letter with the tray still open
phases.soWhat: Repeating a letter adds it again, three is the limit, and three of the seven may not be repeated at all.
phases.concept: A letter may be repeated three times at most

phases.win: the legal pair builds and the illegal one is refused with its reason
phases.does: builds a legal subtractive pair, then tries an illegal one
phases.goal: only six subtractive pairs exist and the rest are not numerals
phases.says: Now put the smaller one on the left. Which pairs are allowed?
phases.check: Write forty-nine as a numeral. Which two pairs did you use, and why not the one letter in front of the fifty?
phases.feels: a lawful pair and an unlawful one look exactly alike until the rail answers
phases.hands: Write the six allowed pairs on the back of the letter card and nothing else, then try to read a numeral built from a pair that is not on the list and see where the reading stops.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which pairs does the card list for the letter in your hand? Second rung, the phase's: is the pair you built one of them? Third rung: the tray offers only the two tiles that this letter may lawfully stand in front of. The list of pairs stays open and nothing built is cleared.

wrong.why: one taken from fifty is forty-nine, and the arithmetic of that is exactly right.
wrong.move: builds forty-nine by standing the one letter to the left of the fifty letter.
wrong.screen: the tile hangs where it was dropped while the refusal strip prints that the one letter may be taken only from the five letter or the ten letter; the reference card turns over to its list of six pairs and the two that begin with that letter light. The rail keeps what was built and the total does not change.

wrong.why: every pair built so far has added, and the two letters look exactly the same whichever side they stand on.
wrong.move: puts the smaller letter on the left and waits for the total to climb.
wrong.screen: the pair is ringed amber and the ledger line for the left hand tile is rewritten with its bar turned back to front; the total drops by that tile's value and the two figures, what it was and what it is now, are printed one under the other beside the ring.

phases.screen: the rail with a smaller tile hovering to the left of a bigger one
phases.soWhat: A smaller letter to the left is subtracted, and only six pairs are allowed: the one letter from the five or the ten, the ten from the fifty or the hundred, and the hundred from the five hundred or the thousand.
phases.concept: A smaller letter on the left is subtracted

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment a fourth tile of the same letter is dropped. It comes down to the rail, reaches the place it wants and stops dead a tile's height above it, and hangs there. The three tiles already down slide apart to open exactly the gap it was aiming for, the rule prints itself under the rail one word at a time, and then the gap closes, the hanging tile lifts back to the tray, and the numeral on the rail is precisely what it was before. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. The tray of seven lettered tiles stands along the foot of the working area with each letter's value printed under it, the build rail waits above with its left hand stop drawn, the ledger beside the rail is ruled and empty, and the reference card of the seven letters is open down the right of the working area on every phase, because nothing here is worked out and it is all looked up. On the first phase the rail is empty; on the second one bigger tile already sits at the left of it with clear rail to its right; on the third three of one letter sit on it side by side; on the fourth one bigger tile sits with clear rail to its left. The running count at the top left reads nothing yet, and the slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the tile in the tray that this phase is about gives one small lift while the voice asks for a tile to be lifted and read. That lift is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any tiles, either direction, with every refusal explained rather than blocked in silence. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, converting both ways and testing where the rules stop.
voiceLines: Seven letters in the tray. Lift one and read what it is worth.
Seven letters, and no more. Find the one worth fifty.
Put the smaller one on the right. Watch the total go up.
Try one more of the same. What does the rule card say?
Now put the smaller one on the left. Which pairs are allowed?
The same seven letters. A different rule.
Free play. Any tiles, either way round, and every refusal explained.
Read the rule card again, and then look at what is already on the rail.
You built numerals, and you found what the rules will not let you build.

observations.why: There are seven letters and no others, and not one of them is worked out from another.
observations.soWhat: This is a system to look up, not a system to reason out.
observations.observe: Every numeral built on the rail came out of the same seven tiles.

observations.why: Position decides whether a letter is added or taken away, and size only decides which letter is the smaller one.
observations.soWhat: One question settles every letter: is the smaller one on the left or on the right?
observations.observe: The total climbed when the smaller tile sat to the right and dropped when it sat to the left.

observations.why: Three rules allow a handful of arrangements and shut out everything else.
observations.soWhat: Knowing this system is mostly knowing what is not a numeral at all.
observations.observe: The rail refused far more tiles than it took.

observations.why: The refused tile never landed, so what had already been built was still correct.
observations.soWhat: A refusal is about the one tile in my hand, not about the work I have done.
observations.observe: Not one refusal ever cleared the rail.

description: Build numerals from lettered tiles, and find out which combinations the rules simply refuse.

mods.learn: Learn, adult alongside. Four worked items, one per phase, ending on the subtractive pairs and what they refuse.
mods.freeplay: Free Play. Any tiles, either direction, and every refusal explained rather than blocked in silence.
mods.practice: Practice, child alone. Eight items converting both ways and testing the limits of the rules.

source_tool.name: Roman Numeral Workshop
source_tool.blurb: Build numerals from lettered tiles, and find out which combinations the rules simply refuse.

serves.exercise: writing the Roman numerals for each of the given numbers
writing the Hindu-Arabic numbers for each of the given numerals
matching the sums of Roman numerals to their values
filling the calendar blanks with Roman numerals
writing the balance in the money box in Roman numerals
ticking the self-assessment list of what you can do

source_tool.description: Seven lettered tiles sit in a tray with their values printed under them, and a build rail waits above. Dropping tiles into the rail assembles a numeral and a running total updates beside it, showing each tile being added or subtracted as it lands so the arithmetic of the numeral is visible rather than recalled. The rules are enforced as the tiles land: a fourth repeat of the same letter is refused, a V or an L or a D dropped twice is refused, and a subtractive pair that is not one of the six legal ones is refused, and in every case the rule that refused it is named on screen instead of a buzz. The rail runs both ways, so a number can be typed and built, or a numeral can be assembled and read. A reference card of the seven letters stays open at the side, because nothing here is worked out from anything else.
source_tool.art_direction: Seven lettered tiles and a build rail / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.
Drawn things, not abstract boxes: token tiles, place value charts with ruled columns, a number line with labelled ticks, digit cards that can be picked up, and lettered tiles for the Roman numerals.

A large number is always shown with its digits sitting in named places, with the period bands behind them and the commas drawn where the Indian system puts them. A bare numeral with no chart behind it is never used to teach place value.
Where tokens or blocks stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A place is told apart by its column label first and by its band colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a token or a place the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The ones period is deep blue, the thousands period is green and the lakhs period is vermilion, and those three bands are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The millions period is rose and appears only where the international chart does. A digit under discussion, or the digit that decides a comparison, is amber. A zero holding an empty place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a period is told apart by its band and its label before its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Read the rule card again, and then look at what is already on the rail.
voice.onNext: The same seven letters. A different rule.
voice.opening: Seven letters in the tray. Lift one and read what it is worth.
voice.onFinish: You built numerals, and you found what the rules will not let you build.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any tiles, either way round, and every refusal explained.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Seven letters do all the work
A smaller letter on the right is added
A letter may be repeated three times at most
A smaller letter on the left is subtracted

placement.where: After the seven letters have been copied onto a card by hand. The tool is what refuses an illegal numeral and names the rule, which a written answer marked later cannot do.

answer_key.rule: Seven letters carry fixed values: I one, V five, X ten, L fifty, C one hundred, D five hundred and M one thousand. A smaller letter to the right of a bigger one is added. The letters I, X, C and M may be repeated up to three times and repetition means addition. A smaller letter to the left of a bigger one is subtracted, but only I from V or X, X from L or C, and C from D or M. V, L and D are never repeated and never subtracted.
answer_key.wrong: The rail keeps what has been built and the rule that refused the last tile stays on screen beside it, so the numeral can be read back against the rule. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Seven letters are used altogether and no others exist.
In order of value they are I, V, X, L, C, D and M.
Their values are one, five, ten, fifty, one hundred, five hundred and one thousand.
items.answer: L is fifty and D is five hundred
items.question: Which letters stand for fifty and for five hundred?
items.checkpoint: Every Roman numeral is built from these seven letters only.
items.misconception: Inventing a single letter for a value that has none, such as one for twenty.

steps: Read from the left. X is ten.
V is five and stands to the right of X, so it is added.
I is one and also to the right, so the total is ten and five and one.
items.question: What number is XVI?
items.checkpoint: A smaller letter to the right of a bigger one is added.
items.misconception: Subtracting the V because it is smaller, whichever side of the X it sits.

steps: Three Xs make thirty, because repeating a letter means adding it again.
Three Is make three, so the whole numeral is thirty-three.
A fourth X is refused, which is why forty is written as ten before fifty.
items.answer: Thirty-three, and a letter may be repeated at most three times
items.question: What number is XXXIII, and why can thirty-four not be written with four Xs?
items.checkpoint: Repetition means addition, and three is the limit.
items.misconception: Writing forty as four Xs in a row instead of XL.

steps: XC is ten placed before one hundred, which is ninety.
VIII is five and three ones, which is eight.
Ninety and eight make ninety-eight. IL is refused because I may only be taken from V or X.
items.answer: Ninety-eight, and I may be subtracted only from V or X
items.question: What number is XCVIII, and why is IL not a numeral?
items.checkpoint: Only six subtractive pairs exist and everything else is not a numeral at all.
items.misconception: Writing forty-nine as IL by taking one away from fifty.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: What are the values of C and of M?
items.final_answer: C is one hundred and M is one thousand

items.question: Which three letters may never be repeated?
A money box holds 1125 rupees and 250 rupees are spent. Write the balance as a Roman numeral.

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: holds the seven tiles with their values printed under them
assembles the numeral from the tiles dropped into it
shows each tile being added or subtracted as it lands
names the rule whenever a tile is refused
turns a number into a numeral, or a numeral into a number
keeps the seven letters and their values open at the side

teaching_notes: Copy the seven letters and their values onto a card by hand before opening the tool, and leave it out. Nothing in this topic is worked out from anything else; it is looked up, and pretending otherwise wastes the lesson. Teach the three rules as one question about position: is the smaller letter to the left or to the right? Then spend the real time on what is not allowed, because four in a row and a doubled V and an illegal subtractive pair are where the marks go. Send them hunting for real numerals on clock faces, chapter headings and foundation stones. This is the closing topic, so finish on the last page of the chapter, where the whole of it is asked at once.
generation_prompt: Build a Roman numeral tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A tray of seven lettered tiles with their values printed beneath them, and a build rail above where tiles are dropped to assemble a numeral. A running total beside the rail shows each tile being added or subtracted as it lands, so the arithmetic of the numeral is visible. Rules are enforced on drop: a fourth consecutive repeat of any letter is refused, a second V or L or D is refused, and any subtractive pair outside I from V or X, X from L or C, and C from D or M is refused. Every refusal names the rule on screen and leaves the built numeral intact; there is no buzzer and nothing is cleared. A direction switch converts a typed number into a numeral or a built numeral into a number. A reference card of the seven letters and their values stays open at the side throughout. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Drag lettered tiles into the rail to build a numeral and watch the total change. Try four of the same letter, and try a small letter on the left of a big one. Read what the rule card says each time something is refused.
